screen: tco-calculator.html v0.8 — input rail restructured around decisions; conversational assist thread on the interview step
notes: Fifth tco-calculator entry and a macrostructure change to the RAIL specifically; the Guided Stepper beside it is unchanged and still governs the top of the column. The previous rail shape was 'noun-grouped field vault with nested disclosure' — six sections named for categories of field (Who uses it, Hardware & prices, Money), three of which arrived folded, and inside two of those a SECOND <details class='adv'>. Routing policy was therefore two disclosures deep, which is exactly the 'buried' complaint. Three changes. (1) Sections are named for the decision they settle, not the fields they hold: How much demand / What the work is / Which model you'd run / What you'd compare against / What you assume about money / Service level & routing, each with the question restated in its hint. (2) One disclosure layer. 'Service level, routing & overlay' (12 fields) was PROMOTED out of Money into its own top-level section — it is not a money assumption, it is the separate decision of what happens when local capacity runs out. 'Architecture detail' (4 fields) became a labelled band (.subsec) inside the model section, because it is the shape of the model chosen above rather than a decision of its own. 'Tokens per turn' KEEPS its <details>: it is a 4x4 table of 16 raw inputs, not a decision, and unwrapping it would put bare numbers in the rail. (3) The fold defaults moved from a heading allow-list in fields.js (OPEN_SECTIONS) to `data-open` in the markup — the old coupling meant renaming a heading silently folded every section, and this revision renamed all six. A test now asserts both directions. Anti-slop on this diff: no new depth strategy, no colour literal outside the token block, no card grid, no icons, no invented number, no new interactive element needing states. .subsec deliberately does NOT get an uppercase mono micro-label: system.md rations those to one per section spine, so the band caption is 11.5px sans in --dim over a hairline. Verified in the server-hosted Chrome at 1920: all seven sections render, the three data-open sections arrive expanded and the other four folded with live value summaries, and the promoted section carries its own summary. eval is unavailable on that browser client, so contrast, 44px targets and narrow-viewport behaviour are NOT pixel-measured this round — they are unchanged CSS from v0.7, which was measured at 390/1100/1920. Also in this revision: the assist ask box left <details class='ai-assist'> and now sits on the interview step with a per-question answer thread, and the vendor name is gone from every UI surface (retained in privacy.html and llms.txt as a disclosure). Next calculator revision should not add a third disclosure layer to the rail.

notes: S9 repeat is deliberate and justified: this is the SAME screen revised, not a new one, so the shape is held fixed and only the argument, palette and small-screen behaviour changed. Three substantive changes. (1) Reading mode: the fixed 1920x1080 stage letterboxed to a 390x219 strip on a phone with 2.6px micro-labels while the nav chrome stayed full size, so the deck read as broken when SENT AS A LINK — which is half its job. Below 1100px it now leaves the stage entirely and renders the same DOM as a scrolling document. This is a deliberate override of slide-design's 'letterbox, never reflow' invariant, which assumes a presentation-only artifact; the reading tier declares its own clamp-bounded fluid scale rather than the enumerated stage ladder (argued V10 + V13). (2) Palette: violet retired — it was borrowed from a vendor relationship that has ended — and replaced with electric yellow #FFE800 as the brand signal, cyan kept for link/data. --warn moved amber -> orange so the clock dot stays a separate semantic against the new accent. tco-calculator.html KEEPS violet; system.md still governs it. (3) Positioning: the deck stopped arguing against systems integrators. Slide 9 became two positive audience columns (infrastructure owner / delivery partner), slide 10 became three negotiable contract shapes with knowledge transfer as an explicit line item rather than an assumed default, and the close moved from 'your renewal date' to 'send me the part that is hard' so it lands for both audiences. screen: tco-calculator.html v0.7 — eight-question guided interview, no credential UI, MiniMax as assistant not driver
notes: Third tco-calculator entry and a deliberate macrostructure CHANGE from yesterday's Conversation-led Cost Ledger: the blank composer was the wrong primary affordance, because an untrained visitor cannot know what the calculator needs to be told. The typed transcript is not deleted — it is demoted into a <details class='ai-assist'> below the stepper, which is where a free-form question still belongs. Restructured WITHIN system.md rather than redesigned: same dark instrument panel, same borders-only depth, same violet+cyan, same mono-for-values rule; nothing in the token layer changed. New components are a numbered 1..8 progress rail whose steps are themselves jump targets, option cards with a selected and a separate is-recommended state (violet marks the visitor's choice; the MiniMax suggestion gets its own quieter border plus an explicit 'MiniMax suggests this' label so advice can never be mistaken for a selection), inline numeric inputs on the three quantitative questions, and revisable answer chips under the stepper. Anti-slop: no wizard progress bar with a percentage, no card carousel, no stepper illustration, no gradient on the active step, no icon set — the rail is numbers and eyebrow words only. The riskiest surface here is the recommendation state; it was given a distinct treatment precisely because a 'suggested' option that looked selected would be an inert-boundary violation rendered in CSS. Verified in hosted Chrome at 390/1100/1920: no horizontal body overflow, all option/nav actions >=44px, contrast holds on the recommendation label. Next calculator revision should not add a third distinct AI surface without retiring one.
